messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Imran was 68 when he first came for help, a divorced South Asian man who had spent much of his adult life working in the nonprofit sector, trying to be useful to others in ways that felt steady and dignified. Long before he spoke about what had happened to him, he described how, since the assault, ordinary moments had become organized around vigilance. He no longer liked being alone in a room or building, and if he found himself without company he would move from space to space as though checking that no one could approach unnoticed. In meetings at the nonprofit office, he chose the chair with his back against the wall so he could see the doorway and the rest of the room at once. He said it was not about comfort but about needing to know where everyone was. At home, after dark, he listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering the house, and sudden noises in the hallway or a loud sound from outside would leave him braced and on edge. If a coworker touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he reacted with visible alarm before he could stop himself, his whole body jerking as if he had been grabbed again.

The event itself had occurred years earlier, after a period in which he had trusted a person he should not have trusted. He did not describe the assault in expansive detail; he said he knew what happened, but when he tried to tell it he could not find the words, as if language stopped short of the worst parts. What he could say was that it involved rape, and that certain sounds from that time had stayed in his mind with unusual force. When memories returned, he sometimes heard those sounds in his head exactly as they had been then, vivid and intrusive enough to make his chest tighten and his body feel as if it were back in that moment. He also reported that the memory did not remain only in his mind: when it came, he felt physical pain in the same parts of his body that had hurt during the assault, a bodily echo that left him shaken and humiliated all over again. Because of this, he had come to dread the memory itself, knowing it could arrive without warning in the middle of an otherwise ordinary day.

In the months after the assault, Imran found himself building a life around these reactions. He was more likely to leave the television or radio on so that silence would not make him listen too closely for a noise at the door. In the nonprofit office, where he was expected to move between small rooms, interview spaces, and shared work areas, he quietly altered his habits so he would not be caught off guard by someone entering behind him. He began declining invitations that would leave him alone too long, including moments when colleagues stepped out and he would otherwise have been by himself in a conference room. He spoke of these choices without drama, but with a weary certainty that they were necessary. He also judged himself harshly for needing them. He had come to believe that his reactions since the event showed he was a lousy coper, someone who should have been able to carry on with more composure. At the same time, he felt that whatever emotional life he had once had had become inaccessible; he said he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, and that there was now a permanent distance between himself and other people, as though he were an outsider looking in on a life that no longer quite included him.

That sense of being set apart had taken a toll on his relationships after the divorce, though he spoke more about isolation than about conflict. He did not frame himself as angry with others so much as hard to place among them, someone who no longer fit naturally into rooms full of people. When feelings became overwhelming, he sometimes hurt himself physically to release them, describing the act as a grim way of bringing the pressure down when nothing else seemed to work. He was embarrassed to admit it and said it left him feeling ashamed afterward, but in the moment it gave him a brief sense that the intensity could be contained. He had delayed seeking therapy for a long time, partly because he had hoped the symptoms would settle on their own and partly because he did not know how to put the experience into words. What finally brought him in was how relentless the fear had become in daily life: the constant listening for danger at home, the alarm when touched, the exhaustion of always choosing a wall seat or avoiding being alone. He came hoping for some way to live without spending so much of the day braced for what might happen next, and fearing that if nothing changed he would remain locked in this guarded, isolated version of himself.
